nameStory: Blue-fruited dogwood gets its name from its distinctive blue berries that ripen in late summer - a standout feature among the many dogwood species. The "dogwood" name itself comes from "dag wood," referring to the hard, dense wood that was once carved into "dags" (skewers) for cooking meat.
description: Blue-fruited dogwood is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall in New England's wetland edges and stream banks. This native shrub produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by striking blue berries in late summer. Like other dogwoods, it has opposite leaves with prominent curved veins, but it's less common than its red-berried relatives.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright blue berries in flat-topped clusters ripen in late summer - the key identifying feature that separates this from other dogwoods with white or red berries

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves are oval-shaped with smooth edges and prominent curved veins that arc toward the leaf tip - feel soft and slightly fuzzy underneath

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters (cymes) in late spring, each flower having four tiny petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub 6-10 feet tall with reddish-brown twigs that feel smooth to the touch when young

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems have gray-brown bark that develops shallow furrows, while young twigs are often purplish-red

habitat: Blue-fruited dogwood thrives in moist soils along stream banks, pond edges, and wetland borders throughout New England. Look for it in partially shaded areas where the soil stays consistently damp, often growing alongside red maple, elderberry, and other moisture-loving shrubs.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in May, followed by clusters of small white flowers in late spring. The curved leaf veins become very prominent as leaves fully expand.
seasonality.summer: Green berries form after flowers fade, gradually turning blue by late summer. Leaves remain dark green and provide good identification with their distinctive venation pattern.
seasonality.fall: Ripe blue berries are most obvious now, often persisting into early fall. Leaves may turn yellow or reddish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare reddish-brown twigs with opposite branching pattern remain, along with small pointed buds. Any remaining dried berry clusters may still cling to branches.

funFact: Blue-fruited dogwood berries contain such high levels of fat that migrating birds can gain up to 10% of their body weight in a single day of feeding - making this shrub a crucial "gas station" for fall bird migration along New England's waterways.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with silky dogwood, which has very similar leaves and flowers but produces blue-white berries instead of bright blue ones. Memory trick: "True blue" berries mean blue-fruited dogwood, while "silky" suggests the paler blue-white berries of its close relative.
contextualKnowledge: Blue-fruited dogwood is sometimes considered a subspecies of silky dogwood rather than its own species, which explains why some field guides may list them together or use overlapping common names. This taxonomic uncertainty means you might see it labeled as either in different resources.
compareHints: Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries. Unlike the tree-form flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, this species is always a multi-stemmed shrub with small clustered flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
